  3. numconv: float64 ↔ string for the JavaScript engine

#numconv: float64 ↔ string for the JavaScript engine

src/engine/numconv is the part of the JavaScript engine that turns a float64 into the string a script sees (String(x), Number.prototype.toString/toFixed/toExponential/toPrecision) and parses a string back into a float64 (Number(s), parseFloat, parseInt). It is written natively in Odin, ported deliberately from QuickJS-ng's dtoa.c (Fabrice Bellard, MIT), and produces the same bytes as QuickJS for every finite f64 and every radix 2–36, so the engine's number output never depends on the C that used to run inside WebAssembly.

It is allocation-free: the string producers write into a caller buffer and return the length, the parsers read a string, and the bignum scratch that the algorithm needs lives on fixed stack arrays (what QuickJS kept in JSDTOATempMem/JSATODTempMem). That is what lets the package build for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with no allocator and no OS.

#Using it

Odin
import nc "wb:engine/numconv"

buf: [nc.MAX_STR_LEN]u8                       // always big enough for any dtoa output

n := nc.f64_to_shortest(buf[:], 3.14)         // "3.14"            (String(x), base 10)
n  = nc.f64_to_radix(buf[:], 255, 16)         // "ff"              (Number.prototype.toString(16))
n  = nc.f64_to_fixed(buf[:], 1.5, 3)          // "1.500"           (toFixed(3))
n  = nc.f64_to_exponential(buf[:], 12345, 2)  // "1.23e+4"         (toExponential(2))
n  = nc.f64_to_precision(buf[:], 12345, 3)    // "1.23e+4"         (toPrecision(3))

v := nc.parse_number("  0x1f ")               // 31   (Number(): trimmed, whole string, 0x/0o/0b)
v  = nc.parse_float("3.14abc")                // 3.14 (longest decimal prefix)
v  = nc.parse_int("0x1f zzz", 0)              // 31   (integer only, 0x prefix, trailing ignored)

For a tighter bound than MAX_STR_LEN, dtoa_max_len(d, radix, n_digits, format, exp_mode) + 1 gives the exact buffer size a specific call needs.

#What matches QuickJS, and how we know

The core (dtoa.odin) is Bellard's bignum algorithm, not a Ryū/Grisu rewrite, precisely so the shortest round-tripping decimal is chosen identically — including the tie-breaking that decides, for a value exactly between two short decimals, which one wins. atod is the correctly-rounded parse (the same bignum, run the other way), so parse_float is round-to-nearest-ties-to-even in every base.

A differential judge (kept out of the tree) compiles QuickJS's own dtoa.c with zig cc and compares the two, byte for byte, over:

  • 2,000,000+ random f64 (uniform random bits), plus every structured edge case: ±0, ±∞, NaN, the smallest and largest subnormals, the smallest and largest normals, 0.1, 1/3, π, e, 1e16…1e23, and thousands of small integers and half-integers;
  • toString in radix 2–36, toFixed/toExponential/toPrecision with every digit count 0–100;
  • atod on the shortest string of each random f64 (round trip) and on 200,000 adversarial strings built from the characters 0-9 e E . + - _ (space).

The result is 0 mismatches. Speed is on par with the C: f64_to_shortest ≈ 1.34 µs/call and atod ≈ 0.5 µs/call, the same as QuickJS compiled with -O2.

#Shape of the port

  • itoa.odin — integer → ASCII (u32toa, i64toa_radix, …), used by the small-integer fast paths.
  • dtoa.odin — the Mpb stack bignum, the pow/log tables, dtoa (the exact equivalent of js_dtoa) and atod (js_atod), with Odin idioms where they are natural (slices and bit-sets for the flags, transmute for the bit casts, intrinsics.count_leading_zeros for clz).
  • numconv.odin — the public ECMAScript surface, including full-Unicode whitespace skipping for the Number()/parseFloat/parseInt entry points.

#Integration

The engine calls f64_to_shortest wherever it used js_dtoa(..., FORMAT_FREE), the f64_to_* helpers for the four Number.prototype methods (the flag mapping is encoded in those helpers), and parse_number/parse_float/parse_int for the coercions. The integer-tagged fast paths (i32_to_string, i64_to_string_radix) cover ToString of an integer Number without touching the bignum.
